extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded researchers, PIs, grant applicants, and study section reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion and informal guidance about how NIH peer review treats revised applications (A1/A2) versus original (-01) submissions, and a proposed policy (roll-over funding) to reduce waste and bias. Relevant to applicants, reviewers, and program officers thinking about fair funding allocation and review behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision bias (preference for revised applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review panels show a measurable preference for revised applications (A1/A2), producing higher scores for resubmissions than for initial (-01) submissions; only about 10% of applications reviewed in normal CSR sections get funded without being revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence can be obtained from CRISP searches by application type/study section; proportions of funding at -01, A1, A2 have trended toward more revising as budgets flatten. The post warns this creates a holding pattern and is not a statement that revised applications are intrinsically more meritorious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the revision process as triage (improper triaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study sections are using the revision/resubmission process to triage and simplify the review workload rather than selecting the most meritorious applications for award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavior is criticized as making the review process easier at the cost of fairness and efficiency; it shifts decision work into later Program pickups instead of honest ranking at the -01 stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfunctory 'will you just fund this' critiques and signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers often write critiques and assign top scores intended to communicate 'Will you just fund this thing already?' to Program staff (e.g., the phrasing 'This more than adequately revised application...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such perfunctory language functions as a signal to Program and undermines substantive critique. Good review practice should avoid using reviews primarily as programmatic signals and instead provide substantive evaluative detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and minimization of wasted effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The current revise-queue holding pattern wastes applicant time, reviewer effort, and taxpayer money (e.g., time spent revising, repeating reviews, maintaining staff and resources while awaiting funding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should consider reducing needless resubmissions to save PI labor and reviewer time; the post highlights real costs like maintaining tech staff, animal lines, and PI effort diverted from productive research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding allocation consistency (IC desired funding target & roll-over)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutes should set a 'desired' funding target consistent with historical performance (e.g., 24% of applications) per Council round and, when budgets are insufficient, roll meritorious unfunded applications into the next round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed mechanics: roll a fraction of prior-round meritorious apps forward (e.g., half roll-over, half from current round) so the A2 that is funded produces similar science to the A1/-01 that would have been funded, reducing needless revisions without changing scientific outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of peer review discrimination (top-20% vs top-10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review systems are reasonably good at distinguishing the top ~20% of applications from the rest but are poor at consistently and objectively discriminating the top 10% from the next 10%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this inherent limitation, study sections often rationally 'protect' near-border applications via favorable resubmission treatment; policy design should account for this lack of fine-grained reproducibility in scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and appropriate use of Program pickups
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmatic pickups (IC picks) can mask study section merit decisions and contribute to the perception and reality of unfairness if used to offset study-section-level triaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post implies pickups should be apportioned transparently and possibly used to support a roll-over scheme rather than to reward perfunctory resubmissions; misuse leads to inefficiency and distorted reviewer incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study-section variability in preference for revision stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Different study sections vary in their relative preference for awarding high scores to -01, A1, and A2 applications; this variation affects applicants differently depending on the study section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and analysts should examine section-level trends rather than assume system-wide uniformity; CRISP or similar searches by study section/IC reveal these patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on limiting number of revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical policy limiting a maximum of two revisions (as of Oct 1996) influenced funding patterns; changes in revision limits (and their enforcement) affect the prevalence of A2, A3, A4 submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that past limits reduced excessive revising and suggests assessing current trends in light of such limits; limiting revisions can curb endless cycles and reduce system inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibility to rank merit at -01 stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should rank applications by scientific merit at the initial submission (-01) rather than using review to preserve or queue near-miss applications for later rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages study section members to focus on honest merit ranking so that deserving new applications can be funded without systemic bias toward revisions; the proposed roll-over policy is intended to enable this behavior over time.
